summary:
The Case Studies section of the Orbital Witness project investigates surface changes in Ukraine by combining NISAR radar, Landsat imagery, and FIRMS fire data. Instead of a broad overview, it focuses on isolating true physical destruction from electronic interference.

The first study examines the Kakhovka basin. After the dam's destruction, the drained reservoir was expected to appear as stable bare sediment. However, the radar showed extremely low coherence. By analyzing the town stability index across fifteen satellite passes, we discovered that these dark radar signatures were heavily influenced by radio interference jamming the signal, rather than just physical ground changes or newly grown woody vegetation.

The second study focuses on Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad. We hypothesized the active front line would appear as unharvested, abandoned farmland. While radar coherence did draw a distinct boundary, polarimetry revealed that intense radio interference actually caused the radar-dark zones, even though optical Landsat images confirmed the fields were indeed abandoned.

Ultimately, these cases demonstrate the immense challenge of using radar in active war zones, proving that electronic warfare and radio interference can easily mask or mimic actual physical changes on the ground.
details:
Orbital Witness tracks the physical impact of the war in Ukraine from space. We combined NASA fire data with NISAR radar images to tell the difference between normal seasonal changes and actual war damage.

To do this, we built a Random Forest machine learning model that filtered over 514,000 fire detections with a very low false-alarm rate. We also measured how much radar echoes changed between satellite passes to see where buildings were destroyed. This gives people a safe, objective way to assess conflict zones where reporting on the ground is impossible.

We built the project using Python and a custom interactive web map. To keep things fast, we used HTTP range reads to pull specific radar data directly from the ASF archive, so we didn't have to download massive files.

Our most creative moment came from a radar glitch. We noticed dark spots on the map where the radar signal failed. Instead of throwing that data away, we realized those spots were caused by military radio jamming. We managed to turn a sensor limitation into a feature that maps active electronic warfare.
